description: Yoko Ono: Music of the Mind traces more than seven decades of Yoko Ono's groundbreaking career, from her early text-based works in the 1950s and '60s to recent large-scale installations informed by her ongoing campaigns for world peace. title: Haruko Tanaka + Reader Chorus documentary
description: Tickets Haruko Tanaka (b. Queens, NY, 1974; d. October 2019) was a Los Angeles–based artist, photographer, graphic designer, and filmmaker engaged in social practice. Born in the United States, she was raised in England and Japan. Tanaka earned a B.A. in Fine Art from the University of Southern California in 1997 and an M.F.A. in Photography and Media Art from the California Institute of the Arts in 2003. Her visual work was exhibited widely at venues such as the Library Foundation of Los Angeles, the Japanese American National Museum, the Museum of Modern Art, CUE Art Foundation, the Torrance Art Museum, and the Armory Center for the Arts. She also screened her films internationally, including at the Rotterdam International Film Festival and the Asian American International Film Festival.

description: tickets Does Your House Have Lions (2021) is a 49 minute film by Delhi-based poet vqueeram and Los Angeles based artist Vishal Jugdeo. Shot like cinéma-vérité, the film is excerpted from an informal archive the collaborators have gathered over their decade-long friendship. Intimate glimpses of vqueeram’s community of artists and activists reveal, in the near distance, an intensification of the Indian ethnonationalist state which bears upon characters in uneven ways. As the camera changes hands between the film’s participants, a shifting, prismatic lens intimates varying degrees of closeness to and remove from crisis. One day in the late sixties, I was on the phone with Rahsaan and mentioned to him that just that day I had bought a house. He responded by asking, “Does your house have lions?

description: Cinema Under Pressure is a Monday night film series at The Wende Museum. It explores the struggles over what audiences are permitted to see. Each screening is paired with a discussion featuring a guest expert. This month’s film is The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp (1943), written, produced, and directed by Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. The story follows British officer Clive Candy across forty years of war, peace, and love. His closest friend is a German officer. Winston Churchill learned of the production in 1942 and asked his ministers to find a way to stop it. The War Office refused to lend the filmmakers military support. Once the film was finished, Churchill tried to block its export. Government reviewers found no reason to suppress it, and the film opened in London in June

description: Tickets Jennifer Doyle reads from her forthcoming book Sex Test. Sex Test makes a counter-intuitive argument for the power of women’s sports. title: Racist by Design: Kelly Lytle Hernández in Conversation
description: Kelly Lytle Hernández launches her new book Racist by Desig n in conversation with Los Angeles Times columnist Jean Guerrero. The book traces the American immigration system from its origins to the way it works today. Most accounts begin with the Chinese Exclusion Act of the late nineteenth century. Lytle Hernández starts a full century earlier, with the Haitian Revolution of the 1790s, which prompted both the country’s first immigration bans and its first refugee resettlement program. She shows how eugenicists and Jim Crow segregationists built much of the current system as expressly whites only, and how Congress amended that system during the Civil Rights Movement while leaving many of its rules intact. title: The Bengali: An Evening of Film and the Power of Storytelling
description: Join us for an evening of film, conversation, and community at the Wende Museum as we explore the stories we inherit, the identities we carry, and the unexpected connections that shape our world. In The Bengali, named one of Nonfics’ Top 20 Documentaries, director Kavery Kaul takes an American woman to India to uncover the past of her grandfather, Shaik Mohamed Musa. He was one of the early group of men who arrived in the late nineteenth century and married African-American women. Her unlikely quest triggers a boldly different encounter between East and West. A personal search becomes a deeper journey into culture, memory, and identity, breaking barriers and building bridges, revealing how histories travel, and families form across unexpected places. Revival_ _Revival makes its path by the sites once home to sacred buildings bulldozed by time and gentrification. With a live sound score, the performance mixes gospel, house music, hip hop, and voice to transmute memory, land, and water into new imaginings, new futures.
